title: FIFA Defiant Over $20 Billion World Cup Investment Plan Despite UEFA's Unanimous Boycott Vote
excerpt: FIFA says it will press ahead with consultations on selling stakes in World Cup competitions even as Europe, CONCACAF, and the Asian Football Confederation unite in opposition.
body:
• UEFA's 55 member nations voted unanimously to boycott all FIFA competitions over the proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a $20 billion subsidiary that would sell up to 20% stakes to private investors.
  • FIFA responded defiantly, saying "Nobody is selling football" and vowing to proceed with consultations, blaming "incorrect media reports" for the backlash.
  • CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation also rejected the plan, while Infantino's senior advisor Carlos Cordeiro resigned in protest.
  • The crisis threatens the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil, the 2030 Men's World Cup co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, and could reshape global football governance.

Europe Fires Back

FIFA declared on Friday it will press ahead with its controversial plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors, even as the most powerful rebellion in the governing body's history gathers force across three continents.

The defiance came hours after UEFA's 55 member nations voted 55-0 at an emergency virtual meeting on Thursday to boycott all FIFA competitions — men's, women's and youth — until the proposal is scrapped entirely. It is the first time in FIFA's 122-year history that an entire confederation has threatened to withdraw from the World Cup.

"Nobody is selling football. This is not something FIFA would ever entertain," FIFA said in a statement released in the early hours of Friday, blaming "incorrect media reports" for derailing what it called a planned consultation process.

"We unanimously and unequivocally reject FIFA's proposal to transfer ownership interests in the World Cup and other FIFA competitions to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale."

— UEFA statement, issued jointly by all 55 member associations

The $20 Billion Gambit

At the heart of the crisis is FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), a proposed $20 billion subsidiary that would take control of the World Cup and other FIFA competitions' commercial and operational rights. FIFA plans to sell up to 20% of FFE to external investors, with Thrive Eternal — a fund run by Thrive Capital, founded by Joshua Kushner, brother of Jared Kushner — expected to lead the investor group. J.P. Morgan is advising on the deal.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino unveiled the plan on Tuesday, just days after the 2026 World Cup concluded in the United States, Canada and Mexico. He offered each of FIFA's 211 member associations $40 million if they agreed to the proposal by September 19 — roughly four times the $10 million they would otherwise receive. Those who reject it, Infantino warned, would revert to the lower payout.

FIFA banked a record $12 billion in revenue from the 2026 tournament. Critics say the body's existing reserves make private investment unnecessary and that the plan is designed to entrench Infantino's power beyond his presidency, which is up for re-election next year. The Times of London reported that a CEO-like commissioner role within FFE could be created for Infantino.

Opposition Spreads Beyond Europe

The revolt is no longer a European affair. CONCACAF, representing 41 nations across North and Central America and the Caribbean, rejected the proposal on Thursday, citing "deep concerns about the lack of due process" and the absence of review by FIFA governance bodies. The confederation stopped short of a boycott but said "football's future — and its greatest asset — must remain in the hands of our football family."

The Asian Football Confederation, with 47 member associations including India, issued a scathing statement on Friday expressing solidarity with UEFA and CONCACAF. AFC President Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al-Khalifa called the lack of prior consultation "totally unacceptable" and said the proposal "cannot realistically achieve the necessary broad consensus" to move forward.

"I cannot stand by while FIFA considers selling a stake in the World Cup. It is a bad deal for FIFA's Member Associations, a bad deal for football, and a bad deal for the long-term future of the game."

— Carlos Cordeiro, former senior advisor to Gianni Infantino, upon resigning

Stakes for the World Cup Calendar

The boycott, if enforced, would have immediate consequences. Six European nations — including host Poland, France, Italy, England, Portugal and Spain — are set to compete in the Under-20 Women's World Cup beginning September 5 in Katowice. The 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil would lose defending champion Spain. And the 2030 Men's World Cup, co-hosted by Spain, Portugal and Morocco, could be thrown into chaos.

European teams dominate global football: six of the top 10 men's and women's teams are from UEFA nations. World champions Spain, along with semifinalists France and England, would all be absent from FIFA competitions under the boycott.

Britain's culture minister Lisa Nandy called the boycott a "principled decision," adding: "Football belongs to the fans, not billionaire investors." Chelsea coach Xabi Alonso, a 2010 World Cup winner, said in Sydney that football must prioritise people over private interests.

What Happens Next

FIFA insists the process is democratic and that it will not proceed without majority support from its 211 member associations. But with UEFA, CONCACAF and the AFC together representing 143 votes — well over half the membership — the arithmetic is daunting. The African confederation's executive committee meets next week, and the Oceania Football Confederation plans discussions in August. CONMEBOL, South America's governing body, has not yet commented publicly.

For India and other AFC nations, the outcome could determine how World Cup development funds flow to football federations in the years ahead. The All India Football Federation, which has benefited from FIFA's existing development programmes, faces a decision with implications far beyond the pitch — one that could shape the governance of the world's most popular sport for a generation.
nri_angle: India's football federation, part of the Asian Football Confederation that has rejected FIFA's proposal, stands to lose or gain from the outcome of this governance battle that could reshape how World Cup revenues are distributed to developing football nations.
